question: Good to see the improvement in the banking core attrition trends here. Maybe we could dig into that a little bit. Takis, I know you mentioned the 4 items. Maybe talk about where you're at with those 4 items that you're talking to clients about. And then, Paul, I think you mentioned a 9- to 12-month time frame for improvement. Is that the right time frame we should think about in terms of getting back to that low single-digit threshold? Any details there would be helpful.
answer: I mean it's pretty much what I said, right? So clients want to know that you give a d***. As my old boss used to say that you are not going to embarrass them in front of your clients -- in front of their clients with outages and other issues and that we are really committed to helping them run and grow their business effectively because we are a critical infrastructure provider to our banks. This is something that the team has started working on from the beginning of the year with better customer service and investments in technology. And I think they're seeing the continuity of that. And that's what gives them confidence that they can stick with us, and we will continue to make progress. So when you look at the actual numbers of what we've seen so far this year, attrition is down 17%. It's down by number of clients and it's down by revenues. The 17% is the revenue number. And everything that we see in front of us points to the fact that peak attrition is behind us. And at the same time, because we have that unique set of products, whether it is Finxact, whether it's DNA, plus all of the surround and Agentic and everything else we can offer, we also see client wins up by more than 50%. The base is much lower than I would have liked, but it's the right trajectory. So what we see in front of us has been a really positive conversation and acknowledgment of the progress that we are making and people seeing the change in the trajectory and the change in how we engage with them. An …
asks: [partial*] Update on the four client-facing items and current progress | [answered] Whether 9–12 months is the right timeframe to get back to low single-digit growth
rationale: They gave timing guidance and some progress metrics, but did not spell out the four items Andrew asked about.
my_note: Confirmed the 9-12 month trajectory with concrete metrics (attrition down 17%, wins up >50%), but glossed over the specific four client items (pretty much what I said).

question: I appreciate how quickly you all are working here. It's great to hear. Just a clarification, if you don't mind, and then a question. Just on the new core banking wins, is it larger deals? Are these broad-based? And how would you characterize pricing? Just trying to understand how the new volume is coming in? And then just my broader question, maybe for Paul, just thinking about the additional $500 million in savings. I heard you it will come beyond 2027, but is there a line of sight into what types of reinvestment you anticipate versus the savings potential that you see? Just want to better understand the logic there.
answer: So on the first one, I would say it's across the board, but a little bit more geared towards larger banks because this is where some of our -- the breadth of our capabilities is a little bit more relevant and a lot of the investments on Finxact, Agentic, et cetera, are a bit more relevant. So I would say we are seeing progress across the board, but more on the larger end of the market. To go back to the question around Elevate, right? So what we've done, just to repeat a little bit, is we've analyzed every noncore asset that we have, we looked for assets that have either economic challenges or technology challenges or overlaps with other things that we do or are not consistent with our long-term vision. And we said, okay, these things attract expenses, attract CapEx, attract resources from the company, and therefore, we need to kind of rationalize consistent with where we want to take the company in the longer term. That, together with the early results that we are seeing from deploying AI is what drove the delta between the $0.5 billion and $1 billion. And it's only been 3 months since last time we spoke. So I would say we need a little bit more time to be much more concrete around what benefit we are going to see by year, leading to that kind of long-term 37%. So we need a little bit more time, and we'll come in the fourth quarter, and we'll be much more specific about at least the 2027 impact. And Tien-Tsin, I would just add on as it relates to any potential investments th …
asks: [partial*] Whether the new core banking wins are larger deals or broad-based, and how pricing is trending | [partial] How to think about the extra $500 million of savings versus reinvestment needs
rationale: They addressed the customer mix of wins, but not pricing. On savings, they gave a general framework and promised more detail later, not the reinvestment/savings breakdown.
my_note: Clarified wins skew toward larger banks, but omitted pricing trends and deferred the specific 2027 savings/reinvestment breakdown to the Q4 call.

question: I wanted to maybe focus a little bit on the Merchant segment. And I hate to ask this, but can you talk a little bit about the trends that you're seeing in Argentina? What's your level of visibility in Argentina going forward and sort of the range of outcomes for this to remain a headwind or stabilize, I think, particularly on the anticipation that I think you noted hit the Clover and VAS penetration. We've been in a lower inflation environment for a while there. So I was wondering if you could comment on whether that activity specifically has sort of normalized. And then how much of a role do you think that will play going forward to the overall results.
answer: So Will, as it relates to Argentina, you saw in our disclosures that it was an increased headwind for us this quarter. I would say that we expect this to be kind of the peak of the headwind as it relates to that dynamic of just the revenue flow-through there. And I would say, overall, I mean, the situation down there economically is one that's still from just an overall volume standpoint is challenged. But this becomes much more of an abating headwind as we move forward, albeit we don't expect this to turn into any type of a growth tailwind for us in the near term. I would just reiterate that this is a great business. We've said that for a long time. There's not a loss component down there. We continue to make a good return. It's just from where it's been to where it is now, it's providing this negative comparative that was more enhanced this quarter, but will get better on the go forward.
asks: [answered*] Trends in Argentina and visibility/range of outcomes for the headwind going forward | [partial] Whether the Clover/VAS-related activity has normalized in a lower-inflation environment | [answered] How much Argentina will affect overall results going forward
rationale: Management gave a clear qualitative outlook: peak headwind now, easing ahead, but not a near-term tailwind. It did not directly address normalization of the specific Clover/VAS activity.
my_note: Stated Q3 was the peak headwind and will abate without becoming a tailwind, but skipped whether Clover/VAS activity has normalized in the lower-inflation environment.

question: I want to follow up on Project Elevate savings guidance increased to $1 billion. Takis, how would you kind of manage customer and revenue churn and disruption as you kind of decommission certain projects and divest certain assets. And then, Paul, you have almost $750 million of add-backs year-to-date and One Fiserv transformation, M&A and other costs. When can we expect those add-backs to start moderating?
answer: Let me start maybe. So as I said in my prepared remarks, I really don't see those things as adding against -- as working against each other. I see them as working synergistically. Like the example that I gave is a real one. Risk holds, the way we were managing that on Clover was through a very manual process. That meant it took a long time to decision whether that was an actual fraudulent activity or it was fine. And that created actually friction for clients. You embed AI and machine learning, you automate the process, you make everything run faster and you need many fewer people to actually touch that transaction than you did in the past. So a lot of the work that we are doing on Project Elevate is around identifying the end state. I gave the example last time of what we are doing with Commerce Hub. You build Commerce Hub so that it replicates the functionality of all of the legacy gateways. And then you migrate clients with very little work on their side because they go to a new gateway that does everything that the old one did. But by the way, it does also a bunch of other stuff much better, including better APIs and better documentation and faster onboarding and better configurability. So I don't see those things as either/or for the majority of the work that is part of Elevate. As I did mention, there are a bunch of smaller products that we have, and there is a ton of them, not a ton of them, but there are quite a few of them. And on those, we are going to be thoughtful …
asks: [answered*] How to manage customer and revenue churn/disruption while decommissioning projects and divesting assets | [partial] When the add-backs / transformation spend will start moderating
rationale: They explained the transition approach and client migration plan, but only gave timing for spend continuation, not clear moderation of add-backs.
my_note: Thoroughly explained how Commerce Hub and AI minimize client disruption during migrations, but didn't answer when the ~$750M in add-backs will start moderating.

question: It's good to see the expected acceleration in merchant in the fourth quarter to the medium-term targets. Maybe help us understand, number one, what was the recurring revenue growth rate had you not had these tough comps from the changes you made still lingering into the third quarter of last year in the Merchant segment, in particular, versus what we saw the negative 3%. So what would it have been positive what, just thinking about the bridge from third quarter to fourth quarter? And then maybe just while you're on the topic, Takis, maybe you could touch on the competitive landscape in merchant just because, obviously, there's been a lot of push by a lot of competitors around incremental POS solutions, and there's been a push for reduced attrition across the industry, obviously. And so I'm curious the conviction that you have in terms of sustaining that medium-term guide for merchant, where is it coming from? What are you seeing from an attrition standpoint in the Merchant segment, in particular with Clover?
answer: Maybe I can start with the second one and then Paul go to the first one. So thinking about our 2 major segments, SMB and enterprise, starting with the enterprise, which is very simple, right? So our existing customer base remains very, very stable with very low attrition. What we have seen, which I talked about a little bit last quarter, since we built our business development team and with Commerce Hub have ready to go, we are seeing a tremendous increase in our pipeline. Obviously, these sales cycles take -- the sales cycles are a little bit longer, so it's going to take some time to show up in our revenues. But everything that we see on enterprise with e-commerce platforms points to a real opportunity there. And we mentioned a couple of the names that we started winning. On the SMB side, obviously, it's a highly, highly competitive market. What we are seeing is pretty much stability in terms of GPV growth, yields and everything else in our business. ISO is growing double digits. ISV is growing, direct is growing and bank is growing. So we are seeing a continuation of the trends that we experienced in the last few quarters. And then what we are counting on is all of the things that we spoke about at Investor Day, which are all of the investments related to value-added services, continued growth of Clover Capital, launching a differentiated high-yield savings account, enhancing our vertical solutions, especially in retail with e-com, the Clover agent and so on and so forth. …
asks: [partial*] What Merchant recurring revenue growth would have been excluding tough comps, and the bridge from Q3 to Q4 | [answered] Competitive landscape and confidence in sustaining medium-term Merchant guidance, including Clover attrition
rationale: Management explained underlying trends and attrition, but did not give the adjusted growth figure the analyst asked for.
my_note: Addressed enterprise/SMB competition and stability in detail, but never gave the adjusted Q3 recurring revenue growth number or Q3-to-Q4 bridge.

question: A question about Clover for Enterprise. Takis, back at Analyst Day, you had decomposed the Clover distribution. You remember this between direct and bank partner and ISV. And how should we be thinking about the distribution strategy for Clover for Enterprise as you roll that out?
answer: It's 2 parts to the answer, right? So one part -- and this is a 2027 thing, it's not a fourth quarter. It's something that will roll out next year. So there are 2 ways to think about it. One is in our book of business, clients continue to grow. They continue to open new stores, et cetera. So we will be able to support them as they continue to expand. And that's kind of use case number one. Use case number two is if you think about some of our larger, for example, retailers, today, those retailers come into Commerce Hub and they take hardware from a third-party provider. From 2027, that will no longer be the case because that hardware can be now a Clover hardware. So there are 2 -- obviously, the Clover value-added services will be less relevant for an enterprise client. But from a hardware standpoint, we will be able to support them in an integrated way with Commerce Hub. So I see it as 2 ways to generate value, the larger end of the Clover segment and continuing to support that and then opportunities to do more revenues at higher margin with enterprise clients.
asks: [partial*] How should we think about the distribution strategy for Clover for Enterprise as it rolls out, including the direct/bank partner/ISV mix?
rationale: Management gave a strategic framing for Clover for Enterprise, but did not address the distribution mix the analyst referenced.
my_note: Outlined two enterprise use cases (expanding existing merchants and replacing third-party hardware via Commerce Hub in 2027), but ignored the direct/bank/ISV distribution breakdown asked about.

question: Really nice to see the stock reaction, well deserved. A lot of times we're getting questions from investors as they get to know you a little better, like who's really -- who's Takis? Are you over the long term? Are you more focused on growth over the long term? Really strong savings margin expansion. So maybe you can give us a little bit of a glimpse into your, let's call it, like long-term philosophy and vision for Fiserv. I think a lot of people would appreciate that.
answer: That's an unexpected question. I've done both in my career. I've done the cost cutting and I've done the growth. And I think you will be hard-pressed to find someone who doesn't enjoy growth and innovation and doing new and amazing things for our clients. In our case, we actually have to do both, and we have to do both at the same time. We need to do the basics right, which means we need to get the company to focus on the few things that are going to drive long-term growth. But in order to do that, you need to eliminate all of the things that are extraction. There are things that kind of made sense maybe a few years ago, but don't make sense anymore. Things that at some point, we thought would grow, but actually have not grown, things that we don't know how to do well. So we need to do those things at the same time. I think Project Elevate simply says that on a static basis, we can run our business $1 billion more efficiently than we've done in the past. But as we do that, that will generate opportunities to come up with new and interesting things about our clients. I think it's very clear in my mind and in the operating committee's mind what are the 2 major drivers of sustainable growth for the company, which is our scale and data and our multiproduct capabilities, but we need to be able to deliver those to the market in a way that's effective and in a way that allows us to monetize our core assets. So unfortunately, right now, we have to do both of those things at the same …
asks: [answered*] Long-term philosophy and vision for Fiserv, including how you balance growth with efficiency
rationale: He gave a clear long-term philosophy: pursue growth and innovation while cutting extraction and improving efficiency.
my_note: Directly explained his dual mandate of cutting non-core extraction via Elevate to fund and monetize scale, data, and multiproduct growth.

question: It looks like a lot of good progress in the banking business. And I think, Takis, you mentioned agentOS has nearly 200 banks now in the pipeline. I'm just curious if these banks are actively budgeting and planning deployments or sort of still more in the experimentation or evaluation phase? And should we think about agentOS as more of a retention tool for clients at this point? Or do you think it's going to be a meaningful contributor to revenue growth over the medium term?
answer: Right now, clients are in the phase of rapid experimentation towards deployment and adoption. It's hard to know exactly how agents are going to play out and how they're going to scale and how quickly. But the way I look at agentOS is in a couple of different ways. First, it's an overall orchestration layer that banks can use, not just for agents, but in the old days, we used to talk about RPA and then about machine learning. So think of it as any -- sorry, any process that you use to automate and streamline and create efficiency in manual processes that you have today. It's going to start with relatively simple use cases that are going to get more complex and more autonomous over time as both we and our clients and regulators get more comfortable with those use cases. But in the interest of being conservative, we start with always human in the loop before we can continue to extend that. So that's one component. The second component is the way we are pricing for agentOS is based on actual value that we generate for clients. And therefore, think of it as a version of tokens, meaning the more you use our platform and the more savings you generate for your bank, the higher the revenues for Fiserv as well. So we are building it in a way where our interests are aligned and the more they use it and the more benefits they see, the higher the revenues that we are going to get. So it's both a stand-alone revenue product. It is partly a retention component, but in my view, it's also a v …
asks: [answered*] Whether the nearly 200 banks in the pipeline are budgeting/planning deployments or still in experimentation/evaluation | [answered] Whether agentOS is mainly a retention tool for clients | [answered] Whether agentOS can be a meaningful medium-term revenue growth contributor
rationale: Management directly addressed the client stage, positioning, and revenue role of agentOS with clear qualitative detail.
my_note: Clarified that the ~200 banks are in rapid experimentation moving toward deployment and explained its usage-based pricing as a standalone revenue driver, not just retention.
